title: IPv4 Addressing: Usable Addresses and Configuration
summary: Calculating the maximum number of hosts, network, broadcast, and first/last usable addresses of a network, and configuring IP addresses on Cisco router interfaces.

content.body:
Quick recap of the IPv4 address classes:

- **Class A** — leading bit `0`, first octet 0–127, prefix /8, host portion 24 bits.
- **Class B** — leading bits `10`, first octet 128–191, prefix /16, host portion 16 bits.
- **Class C** — leading bits `110`, first octet 192–223, prefix /24, host portion 8 bits.

The **0** range is also reserved within Class A, so although Class A is often stated as 0–127, the truly usable range is **1–126** (0 and 127 are reserved).

The number of possible addresses in a network is **2ⁿ**, where **n is the number of host bits**. Two of those addresses are reserved, so the maximum number of **usable** host addresses is:

**2ⁿ − 2**

- **Class C, /24** (8 host bits): 2⁸ − 2 = **254** hosts.
- **Class B, /16** (16 host bits): 2¹⁶ − 2 = **65,534** hosts.
- **Class A, /8** (24 host bits): 2²⁴ − 2 = **16,777,214** hosts.

The −2 removes the **network address** (host bits all 0) and the **broadcast address** (host bits all 1), neither of which can be assigned to a host.

`show ip interface brief` is the quick way to check every interface's IP address and status. Its columns:

- **Interface** — the interface name (e.g. GigabitEthernet0/0).
- **IP-Address** — the configured IP address (`unassigned` if none).
- **OK?** — a legacy validity check; on modern devices you should never see `NO`.
- **Method** — how the address was assigned (`unset`, then `manual` after you configure it).
- **Status** — the **Layer 1** state (up/down/administratively down).
- **Protocol** — the **Layer 2** state (up/down).

**Router interfaces are `administratively down` by default** because the `shutdown` command is applied by default. **Switch interfaces are not** — they are `up/up` when connected, `down/down` when not. If Layer 1 is down, Layer 2 cannot be up; you'll never see `down` (status) with `up` (protocol).

To configure an IP address on a router interface:

```
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
Router(config-if)# ip address 10.255.255.254 255.0.0.0
Router(config-if)# no shutdown
```

Notes:

- `no shutdown` cancels the default `shutdown`, bringing the interface up. You'll see two messages: `%LINK... changed state to up` (Layer 1) and `%LINEPROTO... changed state to up` (Layer 2).
- From interface config mode you can switch directly to another interface (`interface g0/1`) without returning to global config mode.
- Use `do show ip interface brief` to run a privileged EXEC command without leaving interface config mode.
- On a Cisco device you enter the **subnet mask in dotted decimal**, not the `/8` prefix form.

rows: Check status without leaving config mode

content.body:
**`show interfaces`** — detailed Layer 1 and Layer 2 information for an interface (specify one, e.g. `show interfaces g0/0`). Key items:

- `GigabitEthernet0/0 is up` — Layer 1 status.
- `line protocol is up` — Layer 2 status.
- `Hardware is ... address is 0c1b.8444.f000 (bia 0c1b.8444.f000)` — the MAC address, also called the **BIA (burned-in address)**.
- `Internet address is 10.255.255.254/8` — the Layer 3 address.

**`show interfaces description`** — status, protocol, and a **description** column. Descriptions are optional but help identify what each interface connects to:

```
Router(config)# interface g0/0
Router(config-if)# description ## to SW1
```

Remember the difference: **status = Layer 1** (is it shutdown? is a cable attached?), **protocol = Layer 2** (is Ethernet functioning with the neighbor?). And the default state: **router interfaces are administratively down**, **switch interfaces are not** — they come up automatically when connected.

questions.question: PC1 has an IP address of 43.109.23.12/8. What is the network address?
questions.explanation: With a /8 prefix, only the first octet is the network portion. Setting the host portion (the last three octets) to 0 gives 43.0.0.0.

questions.question: PC4 has an IP address of 129.221.23.13/16. What is the maximum number of hosts in the network?
questions.explanation: A /16 leaves 16 host bits, so 2¹⁶ − 2 = 65,536 − 2 = 65,534 usable host addresses.

questions.question: PC8 has an IP address of 209.211.3.22/24. What is the network broadcast address?
questions.explanation: With /24, the last octet is the host portion. Setting the host bits to 1 gives 209.211.3.255.

questions.question: PC5 has an IP address of 2.71.209.233/8. What is the last usable address of the network?
questions.explanation: The broadcast address is 2.255.255.255 (host portion all 1s). The last usable address is one below the broadcast: 2.255.255.254.

questions.question: PC6 has an IP address of 155.200.201.141/16. What is the first usable address of the network?
questions.explanation: The network address is 155.200.0.0 (host portion all 0s). The first usable address is one above it: 155.200.0.1.
